extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in philosophy, media studies, information ethics, and related researchers/policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Conceptual analysis and stipulative definition of 'fake news', distinguishing it from related phenomena (misinformation, satire, false advertising) and identifying features that explain its recent proliferation, especially online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stipulative definition (FN)
rubrics_metrics.description: (FN) "Fake news is the deliberate presentation of (typically) false or misleading claims as news, where the claims are misleading by design."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the author's core proposed definition: emphasizes deliberateness and that the misleading character is intentional/'by design'. It is intended as a working stipulation to distinguish fake news from related phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presented as news / mimics legitimate media
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news "purports to describe events in the real world, typically by mimicking the conventions of traditional media reportage" (Rini) and is "the presentation of false claims... in a format and with a content that resembles the format and content of legitimate media organisations" (Levy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being presented in a news-like format (headlines, layout, tone, supposed reportage) is a central feature — fake news purports to be news, not fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading by design / systemic features
rubrics_metrics.description: The misleading nature must result from systemic features inherent in the design of the sources and channels through which the content is produced and propagated, not merely from individual, accidental errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'By design' can mean either intended misleading content or deliberately deployed processes of news production/presentation that are expected to yield misleading claims; this systemic dimension helps explain recent online proliferation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate intent or foreseeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Purveyors deliberately engage in practices they know or can reasonably foresee will lead to the likely formation of false beliefs in their audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent need not be ideological (e.g., Macedonian clickfarms sought clicks rather than political outcomes); what matters is deliberate engagement in practices likely to mislead or to cause sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likely to mislead a relevant audience / success in uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: A putative item counts as fake news only if it is likely to mislead a relevant audience and typically achieves some measure of success (wide circulation and uptake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Size of the 'relevant audience' is case-specific; mere goal to deceive or mimic news is insufficient without a plausible chance of misleading and some systemic capacity to spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: May be wholly false or incorporate deliberately misleading elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news can be entirely fabricated (fabricated content) or can mix deliberate falsehoods with true elements, or present genuine content with false contextual information (false context, false connection, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws on Wardle's taxonomy and Bakir & McStay's disjunctive formulation: fake news can range from outright fabrication to selective/contextual misrepresentation designed to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation of cognitive biases and heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary fake news frequently exploits cognitive biases—confirmation bias, repetition effects, priming, affective arousal, poisoning the well—to increase belief formation and sharing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online social media amplify these effects ("work on cognitive biases like steroids"); manipulation of heuristics is part of the functional design that sustains fake news propagation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimicking markers/appearance of credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news often mimics the visual and rhetorical markers of legitimate journalism (professional layout, masthead, news-like headlines) to borrow credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digital sharing can remove or obscure traditional credibility markers, making mimicry more effective online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective presentation / obfuscation without explicit falsehoods
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately misleading presentation can be achieved by selective presentation of partial truths, not only by explicit falsehoods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can mislead through omission or framing so that audience forms false beliefs even in absence of outright fabricated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-neutrality (medium of dissemination not decisive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news can be disseminated via traditional news media or social media; the medium alone does not determine whether an item is fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions that equate fake news solely with social media dissemination are inadequate; the critical factors are presentation-as-news, deliberateness, and misleading-by-design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusionary criteria: satire, honest mistakes, and non-news misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire/parody, honest factual mistakes, false advertising, and chronically sloppy journalism are not necessarily fake news: satire intends entertainment/critique; mistakes are accidental; false advertising is not presented as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An item should not be labelled fake news when originators intend satire or when errors are accidental; sloppy journalism only counts if the process is so flawed (and recognized as such) that it is misleading by design. Advertorials that mimic news are a special concern when they erode authority.
